title: Line and Parabola Systems
short: Find where a line meets a parabola by substitution.
trouble: Students stop at the x-values and never find the matching y-values.

blocks.html: A line and a parabola can meet in two points, one point, or not at all. Finding the meeting points combines systems of equations with solving quadratics.

At a meeting point, the same $(x, y)$ satisfies both equations. If both are solved for $y$, the two right sides must be equal there: $x^2 - 2x + 1 = x + 5$. That is a quadratic equation in $x$ alone (substitution). Its solutions are the $x$-coordinates of the meeting points, and each one gives a $y$ from either equation. The number of real solutions, two, one or none, is the number of meeting points.
Set the two expressions for $y$ equal, solve the quadratic for $x$, then substitute each $x$ back (into the line, which is simpler) to get its $y$. Report points.

blocks.title: Two meeting points
blocks.q: Solve the system $y = x^2 - 2x + 1$ and $y = x + 5$.

blocks.title: Tangent line
steps: One solution, $x = 1$, so the line just touches the parabola at $(1, 2)$.

blocks.title: No meeting point
blocks.q: Does the line $y = x$ meet the parabola $y = x^2 + 3$?
steps: Discriminant: $(-1)^2 - 4(1)(3) = 1 - 12 = -11 < 0$, so there is no real solution.
The parabola stays above the line everywhere.
blocks.a: No: the system has no solution.

blocks.html: Stopping at the $x$-values. The system asks for points, so each $x$ needs its $y$. Check each point in both original equations.
